issue_context.title: handler notified multiple times when using include_role
issue_context.body:
##### SUMMARY
When calling a role with `include_role` on different entrypoints (`tasks_from`), handler calls are duplicated.

##### ISSUE TYPE
- Bug Report

##### COMPONENT NAME
handler

##### ANSIBLE VERSION
```pansible 2.10.5
  config file = /etc/ansible/ansible.cfg
  configured module search path = ['/home/duck/.ansible/plugins/modules', '/usr/share/ansible/plugins/modules']
  ansible python module location = /home/duck/.local/lib/python3.9/site-packages/ansible
  executable location = /home/duck/.local/bin/ansible
  python version = 3.9.1+ (default, Feb  5 2021, 13:46:56) [GCC 10.2.1 20210110]aste below
```

##### CONFIGURATION

I got a reproducer without any config change.
```paste below
```

##### OS / ENVIRONMENT
Debian unstable, reproducer using localhost

##### STEPS TO REPRODUCE

The play `test.yml`:
```yaml
---

- hosts: localhost
  tasks:
    - name: "Call main entrypoint"
      include_role:
        name: testrole

    - name: "Call main entrypoint"
      include_role:
        name: testrole

    - name: "Call pouet entrypoint"
      include_role:
        name: testrole
        tasks_from: pouet

    - name: "Call pouet entrypoint"
      include_role:
        name: testrole
        tasks_from: pouet
```

`roles/testrole/tasks/main.yml`:
```yaml
---

- name: "Test main entrypoint"
  debug:
    msg: "main entrypoint"
  changed_when: True
  notify: testhandler
```

`roles/testrole/tasks/pouet.yml`:
```yaml
---

- name: "Test pouet entrypoint"
  debug:
    msg: "pouet entrypoint"
  changed_when: True
  notify: testhandler
```

`roles/testrole/handlers/main.yml`:
```yaml
- name: testhandler
  debug:
    msg: "Test handler called"
```

##### EXPECTED RESULTS

The handler should only be called once.

##### ACTUAL RESULTS

With the same entrypoint the handler call is not duplicated but when using a different one it got duplicated, one per entrypoint used.

```paste below
PLAY [localhost] **********************************************************************************************************************************

TASK [Gathering Facts] ****************************************************************************************************************************
ok: [localhost]

TASK [Call main entrypoint] ***********************************************************************************************************************

TASK [testrole : Test main entrypoint] ************************************************************************************************************
changed: [localhost] => {
    "msg": "main entrypoint"
}

TASK [Call main entrypoint] ***********************************************************************************************************************

TASK [testrole : Test main entrypoint] ************************************************************************************************************
changed: [localhost] => {
    "msg": "main entrypoint"
}

TASK [Call pouet entrypoint] **********************************************************************************************************************

TASK [testrole : Test pouet entrypoint] ***********************************************************************************************************
changed: [localhost] => {
    "msg": "pouet entrypoint"
}

TASK [Call pouet entrypoint] **********************************************************************************************************************

TASK [testrole : Test pouet entrypoint] ***********************************************************************************************************
changed: [localhost] => {
    "msg": "pouet entrypoint"
}

RUNNING HANDLER [testrole : testhandler] **********************************************************************************************************
ok: [localhost] => {
    "msg": "Test handler called"
}

RUNNING HANDLER [testrole : testhandler] **********************************************************************************************************
ok: [localhost] => {
    "msg": "Test handler called"
}

PLAY RECAP ****************************************************************************************************************************************
localhost                  : ok=7    changed=4    unreachable=0    failed=0    skipped=0    rescued=0    ignored=0
```

This happens because the entrypoints are used in the role signature: https://github.com/ansible/ansible/blob/devel/lib/ansible/playbook/role/__init__.py#L157

Two handlers with the same name in two different roles are treated as two distinct handlers. We find unique roles with deduplication based on signature, which includes the `from_` entries (this is what prevents rerunning the same role unintentionally). If the signature differs, it becomes a new Role object.

This seems helpful for a role's handlers for the other entrypoint options `vars_from`, `defaults_from`, and `handlers_from` since these can change the execution of handlers. `tasks_from` may be the exception but I'm also not sure if there are any sensible corner cases that would break if we try to change the behavior.

This is a serious bug. Existing behavior does not match the documentation.

> This approach is efficient, because the handler only runs once, regardless of how many tasks notify it.

@s-hertel There is **nothing** in https://docs.ansible.com/ansible/latest/user_guide/playbooks_handlers.html to the case you've mentioned here. 

Please change the code to match the documentation. I've designed my playbooks around the assumption that handlers only execute once and now I have no idea how to work around this issue.  The closest I can come up with is notifying a handler to install a task in a directory and then looping through that directory in a post_tasks block.  That's a lot of hoop jumping I have to do because the implementation doesn't match the documentation.

Ansible Version: 2.9.27

The bug here is using the signatures + names as the uniqueness.  If the uniqueness was instead determined by the name + content of the task, you'd probably be in a better place. 

I.E.

```yaml
# service/syslog/handlers/main.yaml
- name: reload syslog-ng
  service:
      name: syslog-ng
      state: reloaded
```

Regardless of how many times I notify that handler from anywhere in the execution, I expect it to run once per host per stage.  However, I use this to generate configs for syslog-ng with logrotate entries

```yaml
# service/foo/tasks/main.yaml
- name: Install logging configuration
  include_role:
     name: service/syslog
     tasks_from: local_logger.yaml # this task does the thing and notifies
  vars:
      syslog_program_name: foo
      syslog_log_file: /var/log/foo
      syslog_logrotate: True
```

If I have 8 of those `include_role`'s throughout my playbook, I get the to the main handler phase and 8 times I see:

```
RUNNING HANDLER [syslog : reload syslog-ng] **********************************************************************************************************
RUNNING HANDLER [syslog : reload syslog-ng] **********************************************************************************************************
RUNNING HANDLER [syslog : reload syslog-ng] **********************************************************************************************************
RUNNING HANDLER [syslog : reload syslog-ng] **********************************************************************************************************
RUNNING HANDLER [syslog : reload syslog-ng] **********************************************************************************************************
...
```

That's not what I want, that's not what anyone on earth wants.

> This approach is efficient, because the handler only runs once, regardless of how many tasks notify it.

@reyjrar The documentation you referenced does reflect the code and behavior you show, but it doesn't capture the nuance of how roles work to understand what's actually happening.

(Note: this is an over-simplification based on the reproducer you gave)

Calling a role with a unique signature creates a new in-memory role. If the role is invoked the same way later, the previously created role is reused. Each new role creates Task/Handler/etc objects that are unrelated to those created by a different role invocation. Handlers are scoped to the play, and the last defined by a given name is the handler that will be notified.

Because of the last-defined-wins behavior, when an include_role with a particular signature runs for the first time, it would notify the handler it created (it defined it last), but executing the role again later with the same signature will not necessarily notify the same handler - it will notify whatever handler with that name was last created within the play. If the same handler object is notified multiple times, it runs only once, but 1 physical role directory can result in multiple runtime roles, which may have unique handler behavior based on the invocation signature.

> That's not what I want, that's not what anyone on earth wants.

Even though it's not useful for this arbitrary example, doesn't mean there aren't playbooks that depend on it. For example, a role could manage several services and have a generic handler that restarts whatever service the role was called to manage.

```yaml
# handlers.yml
- name: Restart service
  ansible.builtin.service:
    name: "{{ defined_in_role_signature }}"
    state: restarted
```

That use case would rely on the handler running for each service and changing the behavior to exclude the invocation signature from determining role-uniqueness would break it.

> I've designed my playbooks around the assumption that handlers only execute once and now I have no idea how to work around this issue.

You could work around it by changing how the handlers are defined or how the roles are called.You could add the handlers at the play level and then notify it from the roles. Then all the different role invocations will notify the same handler object.

```yaml
# playbook.yml
- hosts: all
  handlers:
    # contains handler "reload syslog-ng"
    - import_tasks: handlers.yml
```

I think there is a case to be made that if the *only* thing that changes between include_role signatures is the tasks_from entrypoint (which I'm not assuming because your reproducer is incomplete, but is what OP's reproducer shows), that the handler execution will not differ, so there is no need for unique handlers. For example, if an entrypoint flushes handlers, that already flushes all notified handlers, it isn't scoped to the role invocation. Or if an entry point sets a fact that a handler uses, it also isn't scoped to the role invocation. My earlier comment is still the case though:

> but I'm also not sure if there are any sensible corner cases that would break if we try to change the behavior.

I would not be surprised if I'm overlooking a breaking change if tasks_from was removed from the signature.

Getting rid of any of the *other* the role signatures attributes would definitely be a breaking change since they can change what a handler does. I'm not really sure what can be done to improve that (besides redesigning roles in a backwards-incompatible fashion), but it seems like we should elaborate in the documentation to help others avoid running into the same problem.
@s-hertel in my case I did not have any parameter that was an include parameter, maybe local role variables though, but in this case I guess it should be considered identical in all invocations.

So i verified the test case given by OP, also note that if i change ti import_role, the handler only triggers once.

I suspect this is a bug due to the notification matching existing handler that then also gets overridden by handler of same name, probably creating duplicate entries in the code as we allow notifying handlers that "don't exist yet" and can be added later, but before the handler execution.  This would explain why it does not happen on 'import_' as handlers are all defined a priori.

roles are not really encapsulated, which is a common incorrect assumption and why i proposed a 'roles 2.0'. They would have the expected behavior but we would have to keep current roles also for backwards compatibility.
#49338 looks like the culprit, but previous code also had issues

review_comments: Technically we don't need to pass a templar into `get_validated_value` here because templar is used only for `isa=class`. So we could pass `None` instead and save resources by not creating a templar. But it feels like it would result in a fragile code.
